name: Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold
summary: The Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold is a figure-four shoulder lock applied from ushiro kesa gatame, using crushing chest pressure to pin the opponent flat while rotating their trapped near arm behind their back for the tap.
description: Master the Kimura shoulder lock from Reverse Scarf Hold with expert finishing mechanics, grip sequences, defensive counters, and safety protocols.
target_area: Shoulder joint, rotator cuff, and shoulder capsule
overview:
The Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold exploits the unique body orientation of ushiro kesa gatame to create a powerful shoulder lock with favorable grip mechanics. Unlike kimura attacks from standard side control, the reverse orientation positions your hands naturally aligned with the figure-four grip path, reducing the number of grip transitions needed to secure the submission. The heavy chest pressure inherent to reverse scarf hold pins the opponent flat, preventing the hip escape and frame creation that typically disrupt kimura attempts from other positions.

The mechanical advantage stems from combining crushing top pressure with arm isolation. The opponent's near arm is already compromised by the positional control, and the attacker can maintain full body weight on the pin while both hands work to establish and finish the kimura. Common defenses like grabbing the belt, straightening the arm toward the head, or rolling away are less effective because the reverse pressure angle changes the escape geometry compared to conventional attacks.

This submission integrates into a broader attack system from reverse scarf hold that includes the americana, arm triangle, and positional transitions to mount or north-south. The kimura threat forces defensive arm reactions that expose pathways to these alternative attacks, making the reverse scarf hold significantly more dangerous when the opponent cannot neutralize the shoulder lock threat.

injury_risks.injury: Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for strain, 3-6 months for rupture

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training, allowing partner time to recognize danger and tap
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or making any verbal distress sound)
Physical hand tap (multiple taps with free hand)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with either foot)
Any distress signal including screaming or unusual sounds
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure the instant tap is felt or heard
Return the arm toward neutral position by externally rotating back to starting position
Allow partner to self-assess shoulder mobility before continuing
Never release suddenly or allow arm to spring back forcefully
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - rotation must be smooth and controlled
Never use competition speed or surprise attacks in training
Always ensure partner has at least one hand free to tap
Do not apply while partner is in awkward body position that prevents tapping
Never combine with weight pressure that restricts breathing while finishing
Respect immediate taps without testing partner's pain tolerance

variations_and_setups.description: From established reverse scarf hold, control the near-side wrist with your near hand, thread your far arm under the opponent's elbow, and connect the figure-four grip. The standard entry works best when the opponent's arm is already trapped across their body by positional control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent is passive and their near arm is already controlled across their torso

variations_and_setups.description: When the opponent attempts to extract their trapped near arm by extending it away from their body, immediately capitalize by securing the wrist of the extending arm and threading the figure-four underneath. Their arm extraction attempt exposes the limb for the kimura grip.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent actively tries to free their trapped arm from the reverse scarf hold control

variations_and_setups.description: Begin attacking the americana by driving the opponent's wrist toward the mat on the near side. When they resist by pulling their arm upward and away, redirect the energy into a kimura by switching to the figure-four grip on the now-elevated arm.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent successfully defends the americana by pulling their arm away from the mat

attacker.name: from Reverse Scarf Hold Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold with step-by-step grip mechanics, finishing sequences, and counter-responses for BJJ training.
attacker.overview: Attacking the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold requires understanding how the reverse orientation changes grip mechanics and finishing angles compared to standard positions. The attacker must maintain heavy chest pressure throughout the setup to prevent the opponent from creating defensive frames while simultaneously transitioning from positional control grips to the figure-four kimura grip. The key advantage is that the opponent's near arm is naturally presented for attack due to the reverse body positioning, and the chest-to-chest pressure restricts the defensive hip movement that normally disrupts kimura attempts from side control.
key_principles: Maintain heavy hip and chest pressure on the opponent's torso throughout the entire grip acquisition and finishing sequence
Control the wrist first before threading the far arm underneath for the figure-four to prevent arm extraction
Use the reverse orientation angle to your advantage by driving the wrist behind the opponent's back rather than upward
Widen your leg base when transitioning from control to submission to resist bridging counter-attacks
Peel the elbow away from the opponent's body before applying rotational pressure to maximize mechanical leverage
Treat the kimura as part of a submission chain with americana and arm triangle to force defensive reactions
setup_requirements: Established reverse scarf hold with heavy chest pressure pinning the opponent flat on their back
Control of the opponent's near-side arm, either trapped across their body or accessible for wrist grip
Wide leg base with near leg posted and far leg extended to maintain stability against bridging
Opponent's far-side arm neutralized or unable to create effective defensive frames against your position
Your hips positioned low on the opponent's chest to maximize weight transfer and restrict their breathing

execution_steps.description: Confirm your hip bone is planted firmly on the opponent's sternum with your chest driving down into their upper body. Widen your leg base to create a stable platform. Your near arm should be controlling their near-side arm across their body while your far hand anchors on their far hip or belt.

With your near hand, grip the opponent's near-side wrist firmly, pinning it against their body or the mat. This grip must be established before you release any positional control with your far arm. Squeeze the wrist tight against their torso to prevent them from pulling the arm free during the transition.

Release your far-side anchor and thread your far arm underneath the opponent's upper arm from the outside, passing between their elbow and their body. Your far hand reaches through and grabs your own near-side wrist, completing the figure-four lock. Maintain chest pressure throughout this transition to prevent the opponent from creating space.

With the figure-four secured, use both arms to lift the opponent's elbow off the mat and away from their ribcage. This creates the clearance needed for the rotational finish. Drive the elbow upward toward the ceiling while keeping the wrist pinned close to their body, creating a lever arm for the final rotation.

Step your near leg toward the opponent's head to create a perpendicular angle to their body. This leg adjustment prevents them from rolling toward you during the finish and provides the hip angle needed to drive their wrist behind their back. Extend your far leg wide for maximum stability against any bridging attempts.

With the elbow elevated and your base set, drive the opponent's wrist toward the mat behind their back in a smooth arc while keeping their elbow pointed at the ceiling. The rotation should come from your entire body shifting weight, not just arm strength. Apply slow, steady pressure and pause when you feel resistance, giving your training partner time to tap.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds minimum, slow and controlled in training

execution_steps.description: If the opponent taps, immediately release all pressure following the release protocol. If they defend by straightening the arm, transition to an americana or armbar. If they bridge and create space, maintain the grip and follow them, using the kimura grip as a control handle to advance to mount or north-south with continued submission threat.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate response based on opponent reaction

common_counters.counter: Opponent grabs their own belt, shorts, or far-side wrist to prevent arm separation
common_counters.your_response: Drive your chest weight forward to flatten them while pulling their elbow upward with the figure-four. Use short, rhythmic pulls to fatigue their grip rather than one sustained effort. Alternatively, switch to americana by redirecting the wrist toward the mat.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges explosively toward their head attempting to roll you over
common_counters.your_response: Widen your base immediately by extending your far leg. If the bridge is powerful, ride the momentum and transition to mount while maintaining the kimura grip. The bridge actually helps your finish if you can keep the grip intact during the transition.

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens the arm fully to prevent the figure-four from being effective
common_counters.your_response: A straight arm eliminates the kimura angle but exposes the arm for an armbar or far-side armbar. Transition your grip from figure-four to a two-on-one wrist control and begin working toward an armbar by stepping over their head.

common_counters.counter: Opponent hip escapes to create distance and recover guard
common_counters.your_response: Follow their hips with your own, maintaining chest pressure and the kimura grip. If they create enough space to insert a knee, release the submission and consolidate side control or transition to north-south rather than fighting for a compromised kimura.

common_errors.error: Lifting hips off the opponent's chest while securing the figure-four grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent bridges freely and escapes to guard or turtle, losing the positional advantage that makes this kimura viable
common_errors.correction: Keep your hip bone planted on the opponent's sternum throughout the entire grip transition. Use your arms independently while your torso maintains committed weight pressure.

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish by pulling the arm upward instead of rotating behind the back
common_errors.consequence: Reduced mechanical leverage allows the opponent to resist with arm strength alone, stalling the submission and wasting energy
common_errors.correction: Drive the opponent's wrist toward the mat behind their back in an arc while keeping the elbow elevated. The finish is rotational through internal shoulder rotation, not a vertical lift.

common_errors.error: Failing to secure wrist control before threading the far arm for the figure-four
common_errors.consequence: Opponent pulls their arm free during the grip transition, losing the submission attempt and creating space to begin escaping
common_errors.correction: Always establish a firm wrist grip with your near hand first and pin it against their body before releasing your far-side anchor to thread the figure-four.

common_errors.error: Keeping a narrow leg base during the finishing sequence
common_errors.consequence: Opponent generates powerful bridges that compromise your balance and either reverse position or create enough space for guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Step your near leg toward the opponent's head and extend your far leg wide before applying the finishing rotation. This triangulated base absorbs bridging force from multiple angles.

common_errors.error: Rushing the rotational finish without first peeling the elbow away from the body
common_errors.consequence: Opponent keeps their elbow pinned against their ribs, preventing sufficient rotation to generate a tap and stalling the submission indefinitely
common_errors.correction: Before rotating, use the figure-four grip to lift the elbow off the mat and away from the ribcage. Only apply rotational pressure once the elbow is elevated and clear of their body.

common_errors.error: Releasing chest pressure entirely to focus both arms on the submission grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates defensive frames, begins hip escape sequence, and recovers guard before the submission can be completed
common_errors.correction: Maintain torso-to-torso pressure with your chest and hip weight while your arms work the grip independently. Only fully commit both arms when the figure-four is already secured and locked.

training_progressions.focus: Figure-four grip acquisition from reverse scarf hold
training_progressions.description: Practice the grip sequence in isolation: wrist control, threading, figure-four connection. Partner remains passive while you repeat the transition from positional grips to submission grips 20 times per side. Focus on maintaining chest pressure throughout each repetition.

training_progressions.focus: Elbow peel and rotational finish with proper angle
training_progressions.description: With the figure-four already secured, practice the finishing sequence: elbow elevation, base adjustment, and controlled rotation. Partner provides light resistance (30%) to develop feel for proper mechanics. Emphasize slow, progressive pressure with clear stopping points.

training_progressions.focus: Responding to defensive reactions during live attempts
training_progressions.description: Partner uses specific defenses (grip fighting, bridging, arm straightening) while you practice identifying and responding to each counter with appropriate adjustments or submission transitions. Resistance at 50-70% to develop real-time problem solving.

training_progressions.focus: Combining kimura with americana and arm triangle threats
training_progressions.description: Flow between kimura, americana, and arm triangle based on partner's defensive reactions from reverse scarf hold. Partner provides full resistance while you practice reading defensive responses and transitioning between submissions. Focus on making each threat genuine to force real defensive commitments.

training_progressions.focus: Full application from reverse scarf hold with unrestricted defense
training_progressions.description: Start from reverse scarf hold and attempt the kimura against fully resisting partners. Track success rate and identify which defenses give you the most trouble. Adjust your approach based on patterns observed across multiple rounds.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The kimura primarily attacks the shoulder joint through forced internal rotation, targeting the rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), the shoulder capsule, and the glenoid labrum. Secondary stress is placed on the bicep tendon and the ligaments supporting the glenohumeral joint. The forced internal rotation beyond normal range of motion is what creates the submission pressure.

flashcards.question: Why does the reverse scarf hold orientation provide a mechanical advantage for the kimura compared to standard side control?
flashcards.answer: The reverse orientation positions your hands naturally aligned with the figure-four grip path, reducing grip transitions. Your body weight drives directly into the opponent's chest, pinning them flat and eliminating the hip escape movement that normally disrupts kimura attempts. The reverse angle also changes escape geometry, making common defenses like rolling away or straightening the arm toward the head less effective than from standard side control.

flashcards.question: Your opponent grabs their own belt to prevent you from separating the arm - what is the correct response?
flashcards.answer: Drive your chest weight forward to flatten them completely while using short, rhythmic pulls on the figure-four to fatigue their grip rather than one sustained effort. Each pull should be a quick burst followed by maintained tension. If the grip persists after several attempts, redirect by switching to an americana by driving the wrist toward the mat on the opposite side, which attacks a different rotation angle that their belt grip cannot defend.

flashcards.question: What are the critical safety protocols when applying the kimura in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply rotational pressure slowly over 3-5 seconds minimum, never jerking or spiking the submission. Ensure your partner has at least one hand free to tap at all times. Listen and watch for any tap signal including verbal, hand tap, or foot tap. Release immediately upon any tap by stopping rotation first, returning the arm to neutral position, then releasing the figure-four grip. Never test a partner's pain tolerance or hold through a tap.

flashcards.question: How should you release the kimura after your training partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop all rotational pressure the instant the tap is detected. Slowly return the arm toward its neutral position by externally rotating it back to the starting position, never releasing it suddenly or allowing it to spring back. Release the figure-four grip completely once the arm is in a neutral position. Allow your partner to self-assess their shoulder mobility before continuing training. The release should be controlled and gradual to prevent injury from sudden position changes.

flashcards.question: What is the correct sequence for transitioning from positional control grips to the kimura figure-four?
flashcards.answer: First, secure the opponent's near-side wrist with your near hand and pin it firmly against their body. Only after the wrist is controlled should you release your far-side positional anchor. Thread your far arm underneath the opponent's upper arm from the outside, passing between their elbow and body. Your far hand then grabs your own near-side wrist to complete the figure-four. Chest pressure must remain committed throughout this entire transition to prevent the opponent from creating defensive space.

flashcards.question: Why must you peel the elbow away from the body before applying rotational pressure?
flashcards.answer: If the opponent's elbow remains pinned against their ribcage, the rotation is blocked by the structural support of their torso. The elbow acts as a fulcrum point for the submission, and it must be elevated away from the body to create the lever arm necessary for effective rotation. Without this separation, you can apply force indefinitely without generating sufficient shoulder rotation for a tap, wasting energy and giving the opponent time to develop escape sequences.

flashcards.question: Your opponent bridges explosively while you have the figure-four locked - what adjustment prevents losing position?
flashcards.answer: Immediately widen your base by extending your far leg laterally and posting your near leg firmly toward the opponent's head side. Drop your hip weight lower onto their chest to absorb the bridge energy. If the bridge is powerful enough to compromise your base, ride the upward momentum and transition to mount while maintaining the kimura grip. The figure-four grip serves as a control handle during the transition, so never release it in response to a bridge. Their explosive bridge actually assists your mount transition if you maintain grip integrity.

flashcards.question: What submission chain options are available when the opponent successfully defends the kimura from reverse scarf hold?
flashcards.answer: If the opponent grabs their belt or wrist to prevent arm separation, redirect to an americana by driving the wrist toward the mat on the opposite side. If they straighten the arm completely, transition to a far-side armbar by maintaining wrist control and stepping over their head. If they create significant space through hip escape, abandon the submission and consolidate side control or advance to north-south. The kimura attempt should always create reactions that open at least one alternative attack.

flashcards.question: What role does chest pressure play throughout the kimura attack from reverse scarf hold?
flashcards.answer: Chest pressure serves three critical functions throughout the attack. First, it pins the opponent flat, preventing the hip escape that would create space for guard recovery. Second, it restricts their breathing, reducing their ability to generate explosive defensive movements. Third, it anchors your body position so your arms can work the grip transitions and finishing mechanics independently without compromising positional stability. Losing chest pressure at any stage of the attack compromises the entire submission sequence.

defender.name: from Reverse Scarf Hold Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold with recognition cues, escape techniques, arm protection strategies, and recovery paths.
defender.overview: Defending the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold demands early recognition and immediate arm protection, as the reverse orientation gives the attacker favorable angles for grip acquisition. The defender must prioritize keeping the near-side elbow tight to the body and preventing the figure-four grip from being established. Once the grip is locked and the elbow is peeled away from the body, escape becomes significantly harder, making prevention the primary defensive strategy. The unique pressure angle of the reverse scarf hold means standard kimura defenses must be adapted to account for the different weight distribution and escape geometry.
key_principles: Protect the near-side arm by keeping the elbow pinned tight to the ribcage with the hand gripping the opposite shoulder or lapel
Recognize the grip transition early and defend before the figure-four is fully connected rather than after
Use hip movement and angling to disrupt the attacker's chest pressure rather than attempting to push them off with arm strength
Grip your own body, belt, or shorts to create a secondary barrier against arm separation when the attacker begins isolating the arm
Time defensive bridges and hip escapes for the moment the attacker releases positional grips to establish the figure-four
Accept the position temporarily rather than panicking and wasting energy on ineffective escape attempts
recognition_cues: Attacker shifts their near hand from positional control to your wrist, indicating transition from pin maintenance to submission setup
Attacker's far arm begins threading underneath your upper arm between your elbow and ribcage to establish the figure-four
Attacker's weight shifts slightly as they release their far-side anchor to commit both hands to the grip sequence
You feel your near-side arm being pulled across your own body or your wrist being pinned against your torso

defensive_options.action: Grip your own belt, shorts, or far-side wrist to prevent arm separation before the figure-four is fully locked
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker control your wrist or begin threading their far arm underneath
defensive_options.if_successful: Stalls the submission and forces attacker to work to break your grip, buying time for other defenses
defensive_options.risk: Attacker may redirect to americana or use rhythmic pulls to fatigue your grip

defensive_options.action: Bridge explosively toward the attacker's head when they release their far-side anchor to establish the figure-four
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the transition window when the attacker commits both hands to the grip and temporarily compromises their base
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts attacker's base and may create enough space to extract your arm and re-establish frames
defensive_options.risk: If poorly timed, the attacker rides the bridge and transitions to mount while maintaining the kimura grip

defensive_options.action: Hip escape away from the attacker to create distance and begin recovering guard with knee insertion
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker lifts their weight to adjust their base or reach for the grip, creating momentary space
defensive_options.if_successful: Recovers guard position and eliminates the reverse scarf hold control entirely
defensive_options.risk: Attacker may follow your hips and maintain the kimura grip, finishing from a different angle

defensive_options.action: Straighten the attacked arm fully to prevent the figure-four from generating rotational leverage
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the figure-four is already locked but the attacker has not yet peeled your elbow away from your body
defensive_options.if_successful: Neutralizes the kimura rotation and may allow you to pull the arm free from the figure-four
defensive_options.risk: A straight arm exposes you to armbar transitions if the attacker redirects the attack

escape_paths: Bridge and hip escape to recover half guard or closed guard when attacker compromises base during grip transition
Straighten the arm and pull free from the figure-four before the elbow is peeled away from the body
Roll toward the kimura side to relieve rotational pressure and potentially end up in top position if grip breaks

favorable_outcomes.how: Time a hip escape for the moment the attacker releases their far-side positional anchor to establish the figure-four grip, creating enough space to insert your knee and recover closed guard before they can re-establish control
Defend the grip by anchoring your hand to your belt or far-side wrist, stalling the submission until the attacker abandons the attempt and returns to positional control

common_errors.error: Leaving the near-side arm extended or floating away from the body before the attack begins
common_errors.consequence: The attacker secures the wrist and figure-four grip with minimal effort, bypassing the most defensible window of the sequence
common_errors.correction: Keep the near-side elbow pinned tight to your ribcage with your hand gripping your opposite shoulder or lapel at all times while in reverse scarf hold bottom

common_errors.error: Attempting to push the attacker away with arms instead of using hip movement
common_errors.consequence: Wasted energy with minimal effect since the attacker's body weight advantage makes arm pushing ineffective, and extending arms exposes them to isolation
common_errors.correction: Use hip escape and bridging mechanics to create space rather than upper body strength. Hips generate far more force and cannot be isolated for submissions

common_errors.error: Panicking and thrashing when the figure-four grip is secured instead of implementing systematic defense
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion and increased injury risk as uncontrolled movement can accelerate the shoulder rotation beyond safe limits
common_errors.correction: Stay calm and immediately grip your own belt or shorts to prevent arm separation. Focus on controlled breathing and systematic grip fighting rather than explosive escape attempts

common_errors.error: Waiting until rotational pressure is applied before beginning to defend
common_errors.consequence: Once the elbow is peeled and rotation begins, defensive options decrease dramatically and the tap becomes nearly inevitable
common_errors.correction: Defend at the earliest recognition cue, ideally when the attacker first shifts their hand to your wrist. Each successive stage of the attack makes defense progressively harder

flashcards.question: How do you recognize the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cue is the attacker shifting their near hand from positional control to your wrist, indicating they are transitioning from maintaining the pin to setting up the submission. You will also feel their far arm begin to thread underneath your upper arm between your elbow and ribcage. Their weight may shift slightly as they release their far-side anchor to commit both hands to the grip sequence. Early recognition at the wrist control stage provides the best defensive window.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold?
flashcards.answer: Tap early and clearly using multiple signals simultaneously. Verbally say 'tap' while physically tapping with your free hand on any part of the attacker's body or the mat. If your free hand is trapped, use foot taps on the mat or verbal signals. Do not wait for pain to become severe before tapping, as shoulder damage can occur rapidly once the rotation reaches the end range of motion. The rotator cuff and labrum can be damaged before significant pain is felt, making early tapping essential for long-term shoulder health.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the Kimura from Reverse Scarf Hold?
flashcards.answer: The primary defense is gripping your own belt, shorts, or far-side wrist to prevent arm separation before the figure-four is fully established. Secondary options include bridging explosively during the attacker's grip transition window when their base is temporarily compromised, hip escaping to create distance for guard recovery, and straightening the arm fully to prevent rotational leverage. The key is defending early during the grip acquisition phase rather than after the figure-four is locked and the elbow is peeled away.

flashcards.question: Why is the grip transition window the best moment to defend the kimura from reverse scarf hold?
flashcards.answer: When the attacker releases their far-side positional anchor to thread the figure-four, they temporarily compromise both their base stability and their pin pressure. This creates a brief window where bridging and hip escape are most effective because the attacker cannot simultaneously maintain full positional control and establish the submission grip. Once the figure-four is locked, the attacker's control actually increases because the grip itself becomes a control handle.

flashcards.question: What should you avoid doing when the figure-four is already locked on your arm?
flashcards.answer: Avoid panicking and thrashing with uncontrolled movements, as this can accelerate the shoulder rotation beyond safe limits and cause injury to yourself. Avoid extending the arm away from your body, as this helps the attacker peel the elbow and apply rotation. Avoid trying to push the attacker off with your free arm, as this wastes energy without addressing the grip. Instead, grip your own body to prevent arm separation, stay calm, and look for systematic grip-fighting opportunities or bridging windows.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying setup cues and maintaining preventive arm position
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly establishes the kimura grip sequence while you practice recognizing each stage and maintaining defensive arm position. Repeat 20 times per side with no resistance, focusing on identifying the exact moment the attack begins and immediately tightening your elbow to your body.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining grip anchor against increasing resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes the figure-four and attempts to separate your arm while you practice gripping your belt, shorts, or far-side wrist. Resistance increases from 30% to 70% across rounds. Focus on grip endurance and learning when to abandon grip defense in favor of positional escape.

training_progressions.focus: Bridging and hip escaping during transition windows
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the full kimura sequence from reverse scarf hold while you practice timing bridges and hip escapes for the grip transition window. Start at 50% speed and increase to full speed. Track which escape methods succeed most consistently against your training partners.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense with all options available
training_progressions.description: Start in reverse scarf hold bottom against fully resisting partners who attack the kimura. Practice combining recognition, grip defense, bridging, and hip escape into fluid defensive sequences. Assess success rate and identify which defensive responses need additional drilling.
